quote: Yeah. Hey, Tommy. I appreciate you for returning my call here.
stewart_read: The customer just stated his name as Tony Westbrook, and the rep immediately calls him Tommy — a name mismatch the rep never resolves for the rest of the call. This is a callback scenario (customer dialing in after a missed call), which the schema's standard/tesla intro templates don't cleanly cover; the underlying issue here isn't a missing legitimacy statement but a rep who didn't register the customer's self-identification.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be working from a lead record where 'Tommy' is a nickname or alternate contact name and chose to use the record's name deliberately.
coaching_implication: Flag as a listening-discipline gap, not a scripted-intro omission: when a customer states their own name and it conflicts with the lead record, the rep should reconcile it in the moment ('I have you as Tommy on my end — is that alright, or do you prefer Tony?') rather than silently overriding what the customer just said.

quote: Who are you folks based out of? Yeah. We're actually based out of, Utah. That's where I'm calling you from, but we are nationwide and we're local here in, here in Virginia.
stewart_read: Customer runs an informal legitimacy check mid-call. The rep's answer is direct and reasonably specific — names the home state, claims nationwide reach, and asserts local presence in Virginia — which aligns with the schema's honest_specificity pattern even though this isn't the scripted 'how did you get my number' trigger phrase.
coaching_implication: This is a positive moment worth naming to the rep directly: specific, non-defensive answers to legitimacy probes build trust. Reinforce this as the model response for similar questions.

quote: Dominion Energy is what I have. Dominion Energy.
stewart_read: Combined with the name mismatch at 00:06, this is the second lead-record field the customer had to self-correct (utility company listed as Rappahannock, corrected to Dominion). The rep's response — 'Gotcha' — accepts the correction but never flags that two pieces of on-file data were wrong, which is a data-quality signal the design team and closer should have visibility into.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may consider this normal call variance not worth flagging, since utility corrections are common and the customer resolved it himself without friction.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to note in the handoff/CRM when multiple lead-record fields prove inaccurate on the same call — it's a two-minute flag that protects the closer from walking in with bad assumptions.

quote: I think how to do this. I'm, like, 75 years old, so all this technology is way over my head.
stewart_read: This is a direct vulnerability disclosure (age, tech limitation) that the schema explicitly calls a trust gift. The rep's reply — 'Oh, you're good. I can love it. You can also read off those months to me if that's easier' — is a fine practical fix but skips the acknowledgment beat before pivoting to solution.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's fast pivot to the verbal-readback workaround is itself a form of care — solving the problem is arguably more useful to a 75-year-old customer than a verbal acknowledgment.
coaching_implication: Coach a brief acknowledgment line before the fix ('No worries at all, that's really common — let's just do it the easy way') so the customer feels heard, not just routed around.

quote: I'm retired, so it depends on my doctor appointment schedule.
stewart_read: A second vulnerability-adjacent disclosure — retirement and a medical-appointment-dependent schedule — that the rep processes purely as a scheduling constraint: 'Yeah. What what what is that looking like for you right now?' No acknowledgment of the underlying situation, straight to logistics.
alternative_hypothesis: Retirement schedule mention may be read as a neutral logistics fact rather than a vulnerability disclosure, since the customer states it matter-of-factly rather than emotionally.
coaching_implication: Distinct from the tech-literacy moment at 04:33 — this is the second instance in the same call of the rep skipping the human beat. Worth naming as a pattern: this rep defaults straight to task-mode on personal disclosures.

quote: Alright. Kilowatt hours. Alright. We'll start March 2025.
stewart_read: The customer hands over a full twelve months of kilowatt-hour data unprompted and in detail. The rep logs each number mechanically ('Okay,' '386,' 'Okay') without ever reflecting a pattern back to the customer (e.g., seasonal swings) to build anticipation for the design.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be intentionally staying silent to keep the call short per his own framing at 00:27 ('I'll keep this call super short'), deferring any narrative-building to the closer.
coaching_implication: Even a single reflective line ('Looks like your summer months run higher — that's exactly the kind of thing the design will account for') would have created curiosity without extending the call meaningfully.

quote: Perfect. Yeah. Thanks for reading those out to me, Tommy. I'll be able to get this sent over to our design team
stewart_read: The bill figure ($92.08) was captured cleanly at 03:19 but never flipped into emotional leverage — the rep files it toward the design team instead of tying it to the customer's stated motive ('seeing how much it's gonna cost me') or contrasting it against the program's savings framing.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be deliberately deferring all cost/savings framing to the closer to avoid setter scope creep on pricing.
coaching_implication: The flip doesn't require numbers or promises — a single line like 'That's helpful, that's exactly the number the specialist will use to show you where you can cut this down' ties the bill to the reason he called.

quote: I'll get you down for the twenty second at 09:30 in the morning, and, I'll send you a confirmation text with the date and time of the meeting.
stewart_read: The rep locks a specific day and time and promises a confirmation text, covering most of button-up, but never runs the no-driving/computer instruction or the explicit 'is that fair?' handshake before ending the call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's closing tone ('really appreciate your time, and we'll see you next Wednesday') functions as an informal handshake even without the literal phrase.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to add the no-driving/at-computer expectation and the explicit fairness check — schema notes this is predictive of show rate, and it's a 10-second addition that's currently missing.
